takeaways: Prestress stores compression in the concrete; the load must cancel it before tension, and then exceed 0.7√f<sub>ck</sub> before a crack.
Elastic shortening, creep and shrinkage take 150 to 250 N/mm² out of any bonded tendon, so only high-tensile steel near 1400 N/mm² keeps a useful force; strong concrete keeps those losses small.
Pre-tensioning passes the force by bond in a factory bed; post-tensioning passes it through anchorages, with ducts, grout and curved profiles.
The stress, strength and load-balancing concepts are three views of one beam and give the same fibre stresses.
Losses are computed one by one: elastic shortening, friction and draw-in at once, creep, shrinkage and relaxation over years; service checks use P<sub>e</sub>.
Flexural design checks four fibre stresses at transfer (P<sub>i</sub>, M<sub>g</sub>) and service (P<sub>e</sub>, M<sub>t</sub>), then the ultimate moment with the tendon near 0.87f<sub>p</sub>.
An end block needs a bearing check and closed links for the bursting force read from 2y<sub>po</sub>/2y<sub>o</sub>, plus a spalling mesh at the face.
In continuous beams prestress causes secondary moments; a concordant cable causes none, and linear transformation moves a tendon without moving the pressure line.
Partial prestressing lets a member crack under rare full load, with bars keeping cracks narrow, and saves tendons and camber.
bank_note: Long answers on this unit usually ask for a full loss calculation, the fibre stresses at transfer and service of a given beam, the load-balancing load, an end-block design or the pressure line of a continuous beam, each with a sketch. Most syllabi also ask for the comparison of pre-tensioning and post-tensioning and the need for high-strength materials.

bank.q: Explain the principle of prestressing with a simply supported beam whose tendon lies below the centroid. Draw the stress diagrams before and after the load, and show by numbers why the beam does not crack. Take a 250 mm × 500 mm M40 beam, P = 500 kN at 100 mm below the centroid and a load moment of 60 kN·m.
outline: P/A uniform, Pe/Z reverses sign, M/Z from load
Stresses before and after the load with numbers
Decompression and cracking moments against plain concrete
answer: Principle: concrete is weak in tension (f<sub>cr</sub> = 0.7√f<sub>ck</sub>). A stretched tendon squeezes the concrete before the load comes, so the load must first cancel this stored compression before any tension appears. A tendon below the centroid also bends the beam upward, putting the extra compression exactly where the load will cause tension.
Section: A = 250 × 500 = 125,000 mm²; Z = 250 × 500²/6 = 10.417 × 10⁶ mm³. Compression is positive.
Before load the top has 0.8 N/mm² tension, well below f<sub>cr</sub> = 4.43 N/mm². Under the 60 kN·m load both fibres are in compression (4.96 and 3.04), so the beam cannot crack.

Sketch: four triangles or trapezia over the depth, P/A as a rectangle, Pe/Z as a bow-tie with tension at the top, M/Z as the opposite bow-tie, and their sum as a trapezium wholly in compression (draw as in the figure of the basic-principles chapter).
Decompression moment (bottom stress zero): M<sub>dec</sub> = 8.8 × 10.417 × 10⁶ = 91.7 kN·m. Cracking moment: M<sub>cr</sub> = (8.8 + 4.43) × 10.417 × 10⁶ = 137.8 kN·m.
The same section without prestress cracks at f<sub>cr</sub>Z = 4.43 × 10.417 × 10⁶ = 46.1 kN·m, so prestress raises the cracking moment 3 times.

Advantages that follow: the section is uncracked at service (durable, watertight), smaller and lighter for the same span, deflects little thanks to the camber, and resists shear and fatigue better; the cost is jacks, anchorages, strong materials and skilled supervision.

Why the eccentricity matters: the same 500 kN placed at the centroid gives 4.0 N/mm² everywhere. Under 60 kN·m the bottom would be 4.0 − 5.76 = −1.76 N/mm², tension, and the bottom reaches zero at only 4.0 × 10.417 = 41.7 kN·m against 91.7 kN·m with the tendon 100 mm low. The eccentric tendon more than doubles the moment carried without tension, for the same force and the same steel.

Kern: the core of a rectangle reaches h/6 = 500/6 = 83.3 mm each side of the centroid. A force inside the kern gives no tension anywhere; here e = 100 mm lies just outside, which is why the top shows a small tension (0.8 N/mm²) before the load arrives. In a real beam the self-weight moment cancels most of it.
Check: stresses are linear over the depth, so the centroid stress is P/A = 4 N/mm² in every stage, and (4.96 + 3.04)/2 = 4 agrees.

bank.q: Compare pre-tensioning and post-tensioning. Describe the long-line method and two post-tensioning systems with sketches, and say which suits a railway sleeper and which a 40 m bridge girder.
outline: Bond against anchorage transfer; ducts and grout
Freyssinet and Magnel-Blaton (or Gifford-Udall, Lee-McCall) anchorages
Comparison table and choice for each member
answer: Definitions: in pre-tensioning the tendons are stretched between abutments, the concrete is cast round them, and they are released after the concrete hardens; the force passes by bond over a transmission length at each end. In post-tensioning the concrete is cast with ducts, the tendons are stressed after it hardens and anchored at the ends; the ducts are then grouted.

Long-line (Hoyer) method: a bed 100 m or more long with heavy abutments at its ends. Strands are stressed once for the whole line; many moulds sit end to end on it; after steam curing the strands are released gradually and cut between units. Sketch: two abutments, a straight strand, a row of moulds.

Freyssinet system: a ring of wires or strands round a spring, gripped between a female cone cast into the anchorage block and a male conical wedge driven in by the jack. Sketch: cone, wedge, wires, bearing on the end of the beam.

Magnel-Blaton system: wires stressed in pairs and gripped by flat wedges in steel sandwich plates, the plates bearing on a distribution plate on the concrete. Lee-McCall uses threaded high-tensile bars locked by nuts; Gifford-Udall grips each wire with split cones in a barrel.

head: Point
Pre-tensioning
Post-tensioning
rows: full elastic shortening, larger creep and shrinkage
friction and draw-in; smaller time losses

answer: Extension check (both systems): the jack extension is Δ = fL/E<sub>s</sub>. A 30 m tendon at 1395 N/mm² with E<sub>s</sub> = 195,000 N/mm² extends 1395 × 30,000/195,000 = 214.6 mm; a 100 m bed extends 715.4 mm. Comparing measured with computed extension confirms the force.

Choice: a railway sleeper is small, made in thousands, with a straight tendon: pre-tensioning on a long-line bed. A 40 m bridge girder is too heavy to cast on a bed and transport, and its tendon must curve to follow the moment and the shear: post-tensioning with draped multi-strand tendons.
Check on losses: a 6 mm wedge draw-in costs 195,000 × 6/30,000 = 39 N/mm² in the 30 m tendon but only 11.7 N/mm² in a 100 m bed, which is why short post-tensioned tendons need careful lock-off.

bank.q: Why must prestressed concrete use high-strength concrete and high-tensile steel? Support your answer with the order of the losses, taking M50 concrete, E<sub>s</sub> = 195 kN/mm², a concrete stress of 10 N/mm² at the tendon, φ = 1.6 and ε<sub>sh</sub> = 300 × 10⁻⁶.
outline: Losses fixed by the concrete, not the steel
Compare with mild steel and strand stresses
Roles of strong concrete: compression, E<sub>c</sub>, creep, bearing, bond

answer.pre:
elastic shortening  m f<sub>c</sub>     = 5.515 × 10        = 55.2 N/mm²
creep               φ m f<sub>c</sub>   = 1.6 × 5.515 × 10  = 88.2 N/mm²
shrinkage           ε<sub>sh</sub>E<sub>s</sub>      = 300 × 10⁻⁶ × 195,000 = 58.5 N/mm²
total                                         = 201.9 N/mm²

answer: Mild steel (Fe 250) can be stressed only to about 140 to 200 N/mm²; a loss of 202 N/mm² removes all of it. Strand jacked to 0.75 × 1860 = 1395 N/mm² keeps 1395 − 201.9 = 1,193.1 N/mm², 86 percent. So the steel must be high-tensile.

High strength also lets a small tendon area carry the force: 1000 kN needs 1000,000/1116 ≈ 896 mm² of strand at an effective 1116 N/mm², against 4000 mm² of mild steel even at 250 N/mm², which could not be placed in a slender section.

The concrete must be strong because it carries the high prestress compression (often 12 to 16 N/mm² at transfer) in a small section, and because a stiffer, denser concrete loses less: with M30 (E<sub>c</sub> = 27,386 N/mm²) the elastic and creep losses at the same stress would be 2.6 × 7.12 × 10 = 185 N/mm² instead of 143.

Strong concrete also takes the high bearing stress under anchorage plates (limit 0.48f<sub>ci</sub>√(A<sub>br</sub>/A<sub>pun</sub>)), gives better bond so pre-tensioned strands transfer over a shorter length, and has a higher tensile strength 0.7√f<sub>ck</sub> (4.95 N/mm² for M50).

Usual materials: M40 to M60 concrete (IS 1343 asks for at least M40 in pre-tensioned and M30 in post-tensioned work); low-relaxation 7-wire strand of about 1860 N/mm², cold-drawn wire of 1500 to 1700 N/mm², or alloy bars of about 1000 N/mm².

The same point in strains: the total loss 201.9 N/mm² is a strain of 201.9/195,000 = 1.035 × 10⁻³. Mild steel stressed to 200 N/mm² (E<sub>s</sub> = 200 kN/mm²) stores only 1.0 × 10⁻³, so the shortening of the concrete takes away all of it. Strand at 1395 N/mm² stores 7.15 × 10⁻³, about seven times the loss.

Early strength also matters in production: a strong mix reaches the transfer strength in one or two days of steam curing, so moulds and the pre-tensioning bed are freed quickly and the tendons can be released without overstressing young concrete.
Check: 55.2 + 88.2 + 58.5 = 201.9 N/mm², about 14 percent of the strand's jacking stress, inside the usual 15 to 25 percent.

bank.q: List the losses of prestress in pre-tensioned and post-tensioned members, state when each occurs and give the expression used for each.
outline: Immediate: elastic shortening, friction, anchorage slip

head: Loss
Stage
Pre-tensioned
Post-tensioned
Expression
rows: only for tendons stressed one by one
E<sub>s</sub>δ/L; with friction 2pl<sub>s</sub> at the anchor
percentage of initial stress, code table or test

answer: Symbols: m = E<sub>s</sub>/E<sub>c</sub>; f<sub>c</sub> the concrete stress at tendon level, P/A + Pe²/I − M<sub>g</sub>e/I; μ the curvature and k the wobble coefficient; α the angle change in radians; x the distance from the jack; δ the draw-in; l<sub>s</sub> = √(E<sub>s</sub>A<sub>p</sub>δ/p) the setting length with p the friction loss per unit length; φ the creep coefficient (2.2, 1.6, 1.1 for loading at 7 days, 28 days, one year in textbook use of IS 1343); t the age at transfer in days.
Effective prestress: P<sub>e</sub> = A<sub>p</sub>(f<sub>i</sub> − ΣΔf). The ratio η = P<sub>e</sub>/P<sub>i</sub> is typically 0.75 to 0.85.

Why post-tensioning loses less over time: the concrete is older when stressed, so part of the shrinkage has happened and the creep coefficient is lower; but it adds friction and a larger draw-in loss.

Short example (pre-tensioned, f<sub>i</sub> = 1200 N/mm², m = 6, f<sub>c</sub> = 8.53 N/mm², φ = 1.6, E<sub>s</sub> = 210,000 N/mm², relaxation 3 percent): 51.2 + 81.9 + 63.0 + 36.0 = 232.1 N/mm², 19.3 percent.

Short example (post-tensioned friction): a 20 m parabolic tendon with 400 mm sag, μ = 0.30, k = 0.0020/m: α = 0.16 rad, μα + kx = 0.088, so the far end keeps e<sup>−0.088</sup> = 0.916 of the jacking force, a loss of 8.4 percent.

Order of the losses in the pre-tensioned example: creep 81.9 N/mm² (6.8 percent) is the largest, then shrinkage 63.0 (5.3 percent), elastic shortening 51.2 (4.3 percent) and relaxation 36.0 (3.0 percent). In post-tensioning, friction and draw-in join the list and elastic shortening shrinks.

Reducing the losses: stress older concrete (less creep and shrinkage), use low-relaxation strand, stress long or curved tendons from both ends and keep ducts well aligned (less friction), allow for the draw-in in the jacking force, and stress the tendons of a post-tensioned member in a planned order.
Check: the losses are not independent; for an exam the percentages are added at the end, but each must be computed from the stresses at the section, not assumed.

bank.q: A simply supported post-tensioned beam of span 12 m, 400 mm × 900 mm, of M40 concrete, has a parabolic tendon with effective force 1500 kN, at the centroid at the ends and 300 mm below it at midspan. It carries its self-weight and a live load of 20 kN/m. Find the balanced load, the midspan stresses under the full load, the deflection, and the camber under self-weight alone.
answer: Equivalent upward load: w<sub>p</sub> = 8Pe/L² = 8 × 1500 × 0.3/12² = 25 kN/m.
Loads: self-weight 0.4 × 0.9 × 25 = 9 kN/m; total w = 9 + 20 = 29 kN/m. The tendon balances 25 kN/m; the unbalanced load is 4 kN/m downward.
Moment of the unbalanced load: M = 4 × 12²/8 = 72 kN·m; M/Z = 72 × 10⁶/(54 × 10⁶) = 1.333 N/mm².
Deflection under the net load: E<sub>c</sub> = 5000√40 = 31,623 N/mm²; δ = 5wL⁴/(384E<sub>c</sub>I) = 5 × 4 × 12,000⁴/(384 × 31,623 × 24.3 × 10⁹) = 1.41 mm downward (w in N/mm).
Camber under self-weight alone: net upward load = 25 − 9 = 16 kN/m, so δ = 5 × 16 × 12,000⁴/(384 × 31,623 × 24.3 × 10⁹) = 5.62 mm upward (short-term; creep will increase it).

Meaning of full balancing: if the live load were 16 kN/m (w = 25 kN/m = w<sub>p</sub>), the beam would carry a uniform 4.167 N/mm² and stay level. A sag of e = wL²/(8P) = 29 × 144/(8 × 1500) = 348 mm would balance the full 29 kN/m.

answer.text: Stresses under self-weight alone (P = 1500 kN taken as stated; at transfer the force would be larger):

answer: The top tension 1.17 N/mm² is well below f<sub>cr</sub> = 0.7√40 = 4.43 N/mm², so the beam does not crack before the live load comes. At the supports the tendon is at the centroid, so the end sections carry a uniform 4.167 N/mm² and no bending.

Sketch: the beam with the parabolic tendon, the upward 25 kN/m from the tendon against the downward 29 kN/m of load, and the two stress diagrams at midspan (self-weight only: small top tension; full load: trapezium wholly in compression).
Check: both fibres are in compression under the full load, and the average of top and bottom, (5.5 + 2.833)/2 = 4.167 N/mm², equals P/A.

bank.q: A post-tensioned beam of span 15 m, 300 mm × 600 mm, has four cables of 250 mm² each, stressed one after another to 1200 N/mm² from one end. Each cable is parabolic, at the centroid at the ends and 200 mm below it at midspan. μ = 0.35, k = 0.0015/m, draw-in 5 mm, E<sub>s</sub> = 195 kN/mm², E<sub>c</sub> = 35 kN/mm², creep coefficient 1.6, transfer at 21 days, relaxation 3 percent. Find the losses at midspan and the effective prestress.
outline: Concrete stress at tendon level with self-weight
Setting length and slip loss at midspan

answer.text: Concrete stress at the tendon at midspan:

answer: Elastic shortening (4 cables in sequence): (n − 1)/(2n) × m f<sub>c</sub> = 3/8 × 5.571 × 10.868 = 22.7 N/mm².

Draw-in: over the full 15 m, α = 8e/L = 0.1067 rad and μα + kL = 0.0598, so one cable (300 kN) loses 17.42 kN, p = 1.1616 N/mm. l<sub>s</sub> = √(195,000 × 250 × 5/1.1616) = 14,486 mm = 14.49 m, beyond midspan. Loss at midspan = 2p(l<sub>s</sub> − x) = 2 × 1.1616 × (14,486 − 7500) = 16.23 kN per cable = 64.9 N/mm².
Relaxation: 0.03 × 1200 = 36 N/mm².

Why 3/8: m f<sub>c</sub> = 5.571 × 10.868 = 60.6 N/mm² is the loss if all four cables were already in place. Each later cable adds a quarter of it, 15.14 N/mm², to every cable already anchored: cable 1 loses 3 × 15.14 = 45.4, cable 2 loses 30.3, cable 3 loses 15.1, cable 4 loses nothing. The average is 22.7 N/mm², which is 3/8 × m f<sub>c</sub>.

Force profile after lock-off: friction lowers the stress by about 4.65 N/mm² per metre, to 1200 × e<sup>−0.0598</sup> = 1,130.3 N/mm² at the far end. The draw-in pulls the jack end down to 1200 − 2 × 4.65 × 14.49 = 1,065.4 N/mm²; the stress then rises along the mirror line until it meets the friction line at 14.49 m from the jack.

Check: the setting length 14.49 m is less than the 15 m cable, so the far end has no slip loss and the formula 2p(l<sub>s</sub> − x) applies; the total 23.7 percent lies in the usual 15 to 25 percent band for post-tensioning.

bank.q: A pre-tensioned beam 300 mm × 700 mm, span 10 m, of M40 concrete (35 N/mm² at transfer), has P<sub>i</sub> = 1250 kN and P<sub>e</sub> = 1000 kN at 200 mm below the centroid. The total service moment at midspan is 180 kN·m. Find the extreme fibre stresses at transfer and at service and state whether the section stays uncracked.
outline: A, Z and the self-weight moment
answer: Section: A = 300 × 700 = 210,000 mm²; Z = 300 × 700²/6 = 24.5 × 10⁶ mm³. Self-weight 0.3 × 0.7 × 25 = 5.25 kN/m; M<sub>g</sub> = 5.25 × 10²/8 = 65.625 kN·m; the live-load moment is therefore 180 − 65.625 = 114.375 kN·m.
Cracking check at transfer: the top tension 1.57 N/mm² is below 0.7√35 = 4.14 N/mm², so no crack; the bottom compression 13.48 N/mm² is about 0.39 f<sub>ci</sub>, a usual permissible value.
At service both fibres are in compression (3.95 and 5.58 N/mm²), so the section is uncracked and meets even Type 1 (no tension).
Reserve: the bottom reaches zero at M = (4.762 + 8.163) × 24.5 = 316.7 kN·m and cracks at M = (12.925 + 4.43) × 24.5 = 425.1 kN·m, against 180 kN·m applied.

Stress diagrams: at transfer a small tension triangle at the top and a large compression at the bottom; at service a trapezium wholly in compression, larger at the bottom. The change between them is the loss of 250 kN of prestress plus the live-load moment.

Transfer at the ends: near the supports M<sub>g</sub> is close to zero, so the straight tendon gives top = 5.952 − 10.204 = −4.252 N/mm² and bottom = 16.156 N/mm². The top tension 4.25 N/mm² is just above 0.7√35 = 4.14 N/mm², so the end regions are where cracking at transfer is likely, not midspan.

Remedies for the ends: debond some strands over the last metre or two (sleeves), deflect (harp) some strands upward towards the ends, or add top bars near the supports to control the cracks. Each lowers the effective eccentricity where the self-weight moment cannot help.

Loss ratio between the stages: η = 1000/1250 = 0.8, a 20 percent loss, typical of pre-tensioned work. The bottom fibre drops from 13.48 to 5.58 N/mm² partly because of this loss (3.23 N/mm²) and partly because of the live-load moment (4.67 N/mm²).

Largest live load without tension at the bottom: zero stress at M = 316.7 kN·m, so the live-load moment may reach 316.7 − 65.625 = 251 kN·m, a uniform live load of 251 × 8/10² = 20.08 kN/m, against the 9.15 kN/m implied by the given 180 kN·m.
Check: average of the fibre stresses equals P/A at each stage: (−1.573 + 13.478)/2 = 5.952 = P<sub>i</sub>/A, and (3.946 + 5.578)/2 = 4.762 = P<sub>e</sub>/A.

bank.q: The end block of a post-tensioned beam is 300 mm wide and 600 mm deep. A cable with a jacking force of 800 kN is anchored at its centre through a 200 mm × 200 mm plate. f<sub>ci</sub> = 40 N/mm². Check the bearing stress and design the bursting reinforcement with Fe 415 bars, and sketch the end-block steel.
outline: Bearing: A<sub>br</sub>, A<sub>pun</sub>, permitted and actual stress
Arrangement of links and spalling mesh
answer: Bearing: A<sub>pun</sub> = 200 × 200 = 40,000 mm². The largest area concentric with and similar to the plate on a 300 mm wide face is 300 × 300 = 90,000 mm² = A<sub>br</sub>. √(A<sub>br</sub>/A<sub>pun</sub>) = 1.5.
Permitted f<sub>b</sub> = 0.48 × 40 × 1.5 = 28.8 N/mm² (less than 0.8 × 40 = 32). Actual = 800,000/40,000 = 20 N/mm² ≤ 28.8: safe.

Steel: a closed 10 mm link gives two legs, 157 mm², in each direction. Vertical demand 487/157 = 3.1 → 4 links (628 mm²); this also covers the 266 mm² horizontal demand. Alternatively a mesh of 10 mm bars, four layers.

Placement: the bursting zone extends about one end-block depth (600 mm) from the face; place the 4 links at about 150 mm centres starting about 60 mm behind the plate (60, 210, 360, 510 mm), then continue with the beam's own stirrups.

Spalling: add a 6 mm mesh at 75 mm centres just behind the loaded face, and corner bars to hold it; around a single central anchorage a spiral of 8 to 10 mm wire directly behind the plate is also common.

Sketch: elevation of the end block with the plate at mid-depth, compression lines fanning out to the full depth, the bursting zone shaded, four closed links, and the face mesh; a cross-section showing the closed links round the duct.

Horizontal steel: the horizontal legs of the same four closed links give 4 × 157 = 628 mm², more than the horizontal demand, so no separate horizontal layer is needed. Place the bursting steel between about 0.1 and 1.0 times the block depth from the loaded face, that is 60 mm to 600 mm here.

Effect of a smaller plate: with a 150 mm × 150 mm plate, A<sub>pun</sub> = 22,500 mm², √(90,000/22,500) = 2, so the formula gives 0.48 × 40 × 2 = 38.4 N/mm², capped at 32 N/mm². The actual stress 800,000/22,500 = 35.6 N/mm² exceeds 32, so that plate would fail in bearing; the 200 mm plate is needed.

Check by a simple strut-and-tie picture: each half of the force (400 kN) fans out from the plate quarter point (50 mm from the axis) to the block quarter point (150 mm); over a spreading length of about 0.5 × 600 = 300 mm the tie force is 400 × (150 − 50)/300 ≈ 133 kN, the same order as the 176 kN of the code table.

bank.q: A two-span continuous beam, spans 12 m each, 300 mm × 700 mm, has a straight cable with P = 1200 kN at 120 mm below the centroid throughout. Find the secondary reactions, the secondary and resultant moments at the middle support and the pressure line. Then use linear transformation to obtain a concordant cable, and find the prestress stresses at the middle support.
outline: Compatibility at the middle support: R = 3Pe/L
Linear transformation to a concordant cable; stresses unchanged
answer: Primary moment: M<sub>0</sub> = Pe = 1200 × 0.12 = 144 kN·m, constant along the beam and cambering it upward.

answer.text: Compatibility (remove the middle support, put back a force R so the deflection there is zero):
answer.pre:
camber of the 24 m beam under M<sub>0</sub>:  M<sub>0</sub>(2L)²/8EI = M<sub>0</sub>L²/2EI
deflection due to R at mid-length:     R(2L)³/48EI = RL³/6EI
R = 3M<sub>0</sub>/L = 3 × 144/12 = 36 kN (downward on the beam)

answer: Secondary reactions: 36 kN downward at the middle support and 18 kN upward at each end; together they are in equilibrium, as secondary reactions must be.
Secondary moment: linear from zero at the ends to 18 × 12 = 216 kN·m (sagging) at the middle support. Resultant moment there = 216 − 144 = 72 kN·m sagging.

Pressure line: e<sub>p</sub> = e − M<sub>s</sub>/P. At the ends 120 mm below the centroid; at the middle support 120 − 216 × 10⁶/(1200 × 10³) = 120 − 180 = −60 mm, that is 60 mm above (always e/2 above for this case). Between, e<sub>p</sub> = 120 − 15x mm with x in metres from an end.

Linear transformation: keep 120 mm below at the ends and the zero curvature in each span, and raise the cable at the middle support by 180 mm, to 60 mm above the centroid. The new cable runs along the old pressure line; its primary moment equals the old resultant moment, so its secondary moment is zero: it is concordant.

answer.text: Prestress stresses at the middle support (same for both cables, since the pressure line has not moved):

answer: Sketch: the beam with the straight cable 120 mm below, the pressure line rising to 60 mm above at the middle support, the reactions 18 kN up, 36 kN down, 18 kN up, and the moment diagrams (primary −144 constant, secondary triangle to +216, resultant from −144 to +72).

Midspan of each span: the transformed cable (and the old pressure line) is 120 − 15 × 6 = 30 mm below the centroid. Prestress stresses there: P/A ± Pe/Z = 5.714 ± 1,200,000 × 30/(24.5 × 10⁶) = 5.714 ± 1.469, so top 4.245 and bottom 7.184 N/mm².

Check: the kink of the transformed cable over the support is 2 × 0.18/12 = 0.03 rad, so it pushes 1200 × 0.03 = 36 kN straight into the support, the same magnitude as the secondary reaction it replaces.

bank.q: A pre-tensioned beam of span 14 m is 300 mm wide and 850 mm deep, with six 12.7 mm strands (98.7 mm² each, f<sub>p</sub> = 1860 N/mm², effective stress 1100 N/mm²) at an effective depth of 750 mm, in M45 concrete. Find the ultimate moment of resistance and check it for a live load of 10 kN/m.
answer: A<sub>p</sub> = 6 × 98.7 = 592.2 mm². Index A<sub>p</sub>f<sub>p</sub>/(bdf<sub>ck</sub>) = 592.2 × 1860/(300 × 750 × 45) = 0.1088, a lightly prestressed section, so the tendon can be expected to reach its full design stress; the strain check below confirms it.
Tendon force at ultimate: f<sub>pb</sub> = 0.87 × 1860 = 1618.2 N/mm²; T = 592.2 × 1618.2 = 958,298 N.
Neutral axis: 0.36 × 45 × 300 × x<sub>u</sub> = T, so x<sub>u</sub> = 958,298/4860 = 197.2 mm; x<sub>u</sub>/d = 0.263.

Strain check: ε<sub>p</sub> = 1100/195,000 + 0.0035 × (750 − 197.2)/197.2 = 0.00564 + 0.00981 = 0.0155, far past the elastic range (about 0.007), so f<sub>pb</sub> = 0.87f<sub>p</sub> is right and the failure is ductile.
Result: 639.4 ≥ 601.8 kN·m, safe, with a margin of 1.062.

If the moment were not enough, the options are more strands (watch the transfer stresses), a deeper section, or untensioned bars added to the tension zone (partial prestressing), taking 0.87f<sub>y</sub>A<sub>s</sub> into the force balance.

Stress and strain picture: at ultimate the concrete strain is 0.0035 at the top, the compression is the IS 456 stress block 0.36f<sub>ck</sub>bx<sub>u</sub> acting 0.42x<sub>u</sub> below the top, and the tendon force acts at d; the strain in the strand is its effective strain plus the strain added by bending.

answer.text: Service check (P<sub>e</sub> = 592.2 × 1100 = 651.4 kN at e = 750 − 425 = 325 mm, service load 16.375 kN/m):

answer: The bottom tension 2.69 N/mm² is below f<sub>cr</sub> = 0.7√45 = 4.7 N/mm², so the beam is uncracked at service, though it is not a no-tension design. The ratio M<sub>u</sub>/M<sub>service</sub> = 639.4/401.2 = 1.59 shows the reserve between working load and collapse.

Sensitivity to the steel: with eight strands T = 8 × 98.7 × 1618.2 = 1,277,731 N, x<sub>u</sub> = 262.9 mm (x<sub>u</sub>/d = 0.351) and M<sub>u</sub> = 817.2 kN·m. Two more strands add 177.8 kN·m, a little less than in proportion, because the deeper stress block shortens the lever arm.
Check by lever arm: the lever arm 667.2 mm is 0.89d, inside the usual 0.85d to 0.95d for an under-reinforced section.

bank.q: A post-tensioned floor beam shows fine flexural cracks at midspan under service load, although the design calculation gave a small compression at the bottom fibre. Analyse the possible causes, show by numbers how sensitive the bottom stress is to the losses, and state what you would check on site. Take a 300 mm × 700 mm section, P<sub>i</sub> = 1250 kN at e = 200 mm and a service moment of 300 kN·m, designed with η = 0.85.
outline: Bottom stress for the design η
Other causes: weaker concrete, restraint and temperature, overload, misplaced tendon
Site checks: jacking records, extensions, cores, tendon profile, grout
answer: Section: A = 210,000 mm², Z = 24.5 × 10⁶ mm³; M/Z = 300 × 10⁶/(24.5 × 10⁶) = 12.245 N/mm². Bottom stress = P<sub>e</sub>/A + P<sub>e</sub>e/Z − M/Z.

The design (η = 0.85) leaves only 1.49 N/mm² compression; if the real losses are 25 percent the bottom is already in slight tension, and at 35 percent it is at 1.74 N/mm² tension. A small margin at service makes the beam sensitive to every error.

Losses larger than assumed: friction higher than the design μ and k (a badly aligned or dented duct), a larger draw-in than allowed for, early stressing of young concrete (more creep and shrinkage), or relaxation of ordinary instead of low-relaxation strand.

Tension the calculation left out: restraint of shrinkage by stiff columns or walls, and temperature gradients (sun on the slab) can add 1 to 2 N/mm² of tension. Example: η = 0.65 gives −1.74; adding 1.5 N/mm² of restraint tension and a 10 percent overload (1.22 N/mm²) gives −4.47 N/mm², beyond f<sub>cr</sub> = 4.43 N/mm²: cracks.

Other causes: concrete weaker than specified (lower f<sub>cr</sub> and E<sub>c</sub>), the tendon placed higher than drawn (smaller e), heavier finishes or partitions than assumed, or a strand that slipped or broke during stressing.

Site checks: jacking pressure and gauge calibration records; measured against computed extensions (a short extension shows high friction); lift-off tests at the anchorages to measure the force left; cover meter or GPR scans for the tendon height; cores and rebound tests for concrete strength; grout inspection for voids; crack-width measurement and monitoring with temperature.

Remedies: if cracks are fine (under 0.2 mm) and stable, record and monitor, since the member may still satisfy Type 3; otherwise add external prestress or bonded plates, and seal the cracks against corrosion.

Reading the crack pattern first: vertical cracks at midspan, widest at the soffit and closing upward, point to flexure (too little prestress or too much moment); cracks running along the tendon line point to a duct, grout or bursting problem; inclined cracks near the supports point to shear. Map the cracks, their widths and their change with load and temperature before choosing tests.

Order of investigation: drawings and stressing records first (cheap), then non-destructive checks of cover, tendon height and concrete strength, then lift-off tests and, if needed, a load test with deflection and crack-width readings. Each step narrows the cause before any repair is chosen.
Check of the sensitivity: each 0.1 drop in η removes 0.1 × 1250 × (1/A + e/Z) = 125,000 × (4.76 × 10⁻⁶ + 8.16 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.62 N/mm² from the bottom fibre, which matches the steps in the table.

bank.q: For a building floor beam 350 mm × 750 mm of M40 concrete, span 10 m, dead load 10 kN/m (including self-weight) and live load 15 kN/m, compare a fully prestressed design (no tension under full load) with a partially prestressed design (decompression under dead load, bars for strength). Tendons at e = 275 mm (d<sub>p</sub> = 650 mm), 12.7 mm strands at an effective 1116 N/mm², bars Fe 500 at d<sub>s</sub> = 700 mm. Discuss which you would choose.
outline: Prestress needed for each design and number of strands
Service stresses and degree of prestressing
Ultimate strength; bars needed for the partial design
Camber and deflection under dead load
answer: Section: A = 262,500 mm², Z = 350 × 750²/6 = 32.81 × 10⁶ mm³, Z/A = 125 mm, e = 275 mm. Moments: M<sub>d</sub> = 10 × 10²/8 = 125 kN·m; M<sub>l</sub> = 15 × 10²/8 = 187.5 kN·m; total 312.5 kN·m. Each strand gives 98.7 × 1116 = 110.15 kN.
Full prestressing (bottom stress ≥ 0 at 312.5 kN·m): P<sub>e</sub> ≥ M/(Z/A + e) = 312.5 × 10⁶/400 = 781.2 kN → 7.09 → 8 strands (881.2 kN).

Partial prestressing (decompression under dead load): P<sub>e</sub> ≥ 125 × 10⁶/400 = 312.5 kN → 3 strands (330.4 kN). Under full load the bottom stress is 1.259 + 2.769 − 9.524 = −5.5 N/mm², more tension than f<sub>cr</sub> = 4.43: it cracks under full live load (Type 3), λ = 0.42.

Ultimate (M<sub>u</sub> required = 1.5 × 312.5 = 468.75 kN·m). Full: T = 8 × 98.7 × 1618.2 = 1,277.7 kN, x<sub>u</sub> = 253.5 mm, M<sub>u</sub> ≈ 694 kN·m, far more than needed (index 0.16, so the code table would trim f<sub>pb</sub> slightly).

Partial: strands give T<sub>p</sub> = 479.1 kN; solving 0.36 × 40 × 350 x<sub>u</sub> = T<sub>p</sub> + T<sub>s</sub> with M<sub>u</sub> = T<sub>p</sub>(650 − 0.42x<sub>u</sub>) + T<sub>s</sub>(700 − 0.42x<sub>u</sub>) = 468.75 kN·m gives T<sub>s</sub> = 296.3 kN, x<sub>u</sub> = 153.9 mm, A<sub>s</sub> = 296,306/435 = 681 mm²: provide 3 bars of 18 mm (763 mm²).

Dead-load deflection with parabolic tendons: w<sub>p</sub> = 8P<sub>e</sub>e/L² = 19.39 kN/m (full) and 7.27 kN/m (partial) against 10 kN/m. With E<sub>c</sub> = 31,623 N/mm² and I = 12.3 × 10⁹ mm⁴, the full design cambers 3.1 mm upward and the partial design sags 0.9 mm, before creep (which can multiply both by about 2.5).

Evaluation: in a building the full live load is rare, the floor is indoors, and fine cracks that close when the load goes are acceptable. Full prestressing would carry an excess of strength, a permanent upward camber that creep enlarges (cracking finishes), and more anchorages. The partial design balances the dead load, keeps the floor level, is cheaper and more ductile.

Recommendation: partial prestressing, with the crack width checked (0.2 mm limit for ordinary exposure) and the deflection under live load checked on the cracked section. Full prestressing would be chosen instead for a water tank, a member in aggressive exposure or one under repeated heavy load where fatigue of cracked strand matters.
Check: partial design force balance 479.1 + 296.3 = 775.5 kN = 0.36 × 40 × 350 × 153.9/1000 = 775.5 kN.

glossary.def: Concrete in which compression has been introduced before loading, by stretched high-tensile steel, to counter the tension the loads will cause.
A wire, strand, bar or group of them that carries the prestressing force.
Wires twisted together; the 7-wire strand has six wires round a centre wire.
The tendon force while the jack holds it, before any loss.
The handing of the prestress to the concrete: release from the bed in pre-tensioning, lock-off at the anchorage in post-tensioning.
The force left in the tendon after all losses; used for service checks.
η = P<sub>e</sub>/P<sub>i</sub>, typically 0.75 to 0.85.
The moment at which the stress at the tension face just falls to zero.
The moment at which the tension face reaches the modulus of rupture.
Distance from the centroid of the concrete section to the tendon.
The line of action of the resultant compression in the concrete along the member.
Choosing a tendon profile whose upward push cancels part or all of the downward load.
The length over which a pre-tensioned tendon passes its force to the concrete by bond.
A sheath cast into the concrete to leave a passage for a post-tensioned tendon.
Pumping cement grout into the duct after stressing, for bond and corrosion protection.
The device of wedges, plates or nuts that holds a stressed tendon against the concrete.
The movement of the wedges into the anchorage at lock-off, which shortens the tendon.
The length from the anchor over which draw-in is used up by reverse friction.
Loss of stress in steel held at constant length.
Growth of strain in concrete under sustained stress.
Shortening of concrete as it dries, independent of load.
The anchorage zone near a post-tensioned anchorage, about one member depth long, where the force spreads.
Transverse tension inside the end block caused by the spreading of the anchorage force.
Local tension near the loaded face round the plate edges and between anchorages.
The moment in a continuous member caused by the support reactions that prestress induces.
A cable in a continuous member that causes no secondary moments, so the pressure line follows it.
Moving a cable at the intermediate supports without changing its end positions or its curvature in each span; the pressure line stays put.
Prestressing that allows cracks of limited width under full service load, with untensioned bars added (Type 3).
